paras: The dynamiting of the Black Baptist church at Carlisle, Indiana, took place early on August 25, 1905, when dynamite placed under the altar destroyed the building. Dispatches from Vincennes described it as the result of a "race war" in the town and reported threats that every Black resident would be driven out if anyone was arrested. The wire story ran in papers across the country, and several Southern editors cited it to accuse Northern papers of ignoring violence outside the South.

Every account treats the bombing as the outcome of a racial conflict already under way in Carlisle; the news reached the press through dispatches from Vincennes. The Louisville Courier-Journal described a "race war that has prevailed for some time," and the Adair County News wrote that it had "prevailed for quite a while." None of the coverage says what the earlier trouble consisted of.

According to the Vincennes dispatch of August 25, the church was destroyed "early today" by dynamite placed under the altar. The Courier-Journal said the building was "totally destroyed," and the Adair County News said it was "blown to pieces." No deaths or injuries were reported.

Bloodhounds were then put on the trail of the dynamiters, whom the wire did not identify. At the same time, threats were made that "every negro in town" would be driven out if any arrests took place. The Pickens Sentinel-Journal and the Fredericksburg Free Lance said these threats came from "the whites."

No report of arrests, an inquest, a grand jury inquiry or the identity of the dynamiters appears in the coverage through the end of September. Nor does the coverage say whether Black residents left Carlisle or whether the congregation rebuilt.

The Associated Press wire from Vincennes, dated August 25, ran that day and the next in papers including the Marshalltown Evening Times-Republican, the Minneapolis Journal, the New-York Tribune, the Washington Evening Star, the Birmingham Age-Herald and the Richmond Times Dispatch. Most headlines were plain, such as "Negro Church Blown Up" or "Threatening Race War," and the wire text assigned no race to the dynamiters. The Rock Island Argus was an exception, heading the story "Whites Blow Up a Negro Church." Reprints and rewrites continued into early September in papers from Indiana and Ohio to Texas and North Dakota, some carrying dates of August 26 or 27.

Southern papers turned the story into a point about Northern coverage. The Alexandria Gazette said the "outrage" got "a few lines in the northern papers" but would have drawn "scare" headlines had it happened in the South. The Adair County News in Kentucky wrote that little importance was attached to it "since it did not happen in the South," claimed that no such destruction had occurred south of the Ohio, and concluded that "The negro's best friends are southern people." The Fredericksburg Free Lance called it a "genuine race war" and "wanton destruction," pointedly placing it "in the Republican State of Indiana" near the home of Vice-President Fairbanks.

In the Black press, the Washington Bee and the Richmond Planet both carried the story on September 2 as short wire items among other news, without comment. The Bee wrote that the church was destroyed "one day last week," while the Planet listed it in its weekly news digest under Saturday, August 26. Neither Black paper took up the regional argument that the Southern editors made.

The papers printed on August 25 and 26 place the bombing early on August 25, which makes them the best evidence for the date. A later version datelined Vincennes, August 27, said the church was destroyed "yesterday," and the Richmond Planet entered it under August 26; these later dates appear to follow re-dated wire copy rather than separate reports.

reader.title: Dynamiting of the Black Baptist church at Carlisle, Indiana
bases: The core act reported is the destruction of the Black Baptist church by dynamite, accompanied by threats to expel Black residents if arrests were made (A1, A3, A5).

Many papers carried the same Vincennes wire (A1, A3, A4), and a separately worded summary brief (A5) and both Black papers (A23, A24) agree on the dynamiting, but every account traces to dispatches from Vincennes and no local or follow-up report was found.

accounts.gist: As the result of a race war at Carlisle, the Black Baptist church was destroyed early in the day by dynamite placed under the altar; bloodhounds were set on the dynamiters' trail and threats were made to drive out every Black resident if arrests followed.

accounts.label: Louisville Courier-Journal summary
accounts.gist: Describes a race war 'that has prevailed for some time' and says the church was 'totally destroyed'.

accounts.label: Southern editorial comment
accounts.gist: Says the act was done by whites and that Northern papers gave it little space, contrasting it with their coverage of Southern violence.

accounts.label: Black weekly news briefs
accounts.gist: Restate the wire without comment, one dating it 'one day last week' and the other listing it under August 26.

framing.detail: Most papers ran the wire under headlines such as 'Negro Church Blown Up' and 'Threatening Race War', without assigning blame.
The Rock Island Argus headline 'Whites Blow Up a Negro Church' named the perpetrators' race outright.

Southern editorials called it an 'outrage' and 'wanton destruction' but used it chiefly to charge Northern papers with a double standard; the Adair County News added that 'The negro's best friends are southern people.'
The Washington Bee and Richmond Planet carried one-sentence or short wire briefs among other news with no editorial comment.
